t: Smallest Unique Subarray — Binary Search on Answer with Rolling Hash
o: We need the smallest length $L$ such that **some** contiguous subarray of length $L$ appears exactly once in `nums`. In example 3, every value repeats at length 1, but at length 2 all four windows are distinct, so the answer is 2. The key structural fact is **monotonicity**: if a subarray $S$ of length $L$ is unique, then any extension of $S$ is also unique — a duplicate of the extension would contain a duplicate of $S$. Hence "a unique subarray of length $L$ exists" is a monotone predicate, so we can binary search on $L$. With $n \le 10^5$, comparing windows naively costs $O(n)$ each, giving $O(n^2)$ total — acceptable only for a brute-force baseline. The efficient check compares all $n-L+1$ windows in $O(n)$ using polynomial rolling hashes.
k: Monotonicity: any superstring of a unique subarray is itself unique, so the answer admits binary search over length.
Rolling hash lets us compare all windows of a fixed length in O(n); use two independent mods (or a huge prime modulus) to make collisions negligible.
The answer always exists since the whole array is trivially a unique subarray.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force by Increasing Length
a.i: Try each length $L = 1, 2, \dots$ in order and count every window of that length using a hash map keyed by the window contents (as a tuple/string). The first $L$ where some window has count 1 is the answer. Correctness follows directly from the definition, and starting from small $L$ means we stop early when the answer is tiny.
s: Build a dictionary mapping each window of length L (stored as a tuple or joined string) to its occurrence count.
If any key has count exactly 1, return L.
Return n if no smaller length works (the full array is always unique).
a.t: O(n^2) expected time — there can be up to n distinct lengths and building/counting windows of length L costs O(n·L) for hashing keys; fine for small inputs but too slow at the constraint limit in adversarial cases.
a.sp: O(n^2) worst case — the hash map may hold up to n windows each of length L (e.g., storing strings).

a.n: Approach 2: Binary Search on Length + Rolling Hash (Optimal)
a.i: Because uniqueness-by-extension is monotone, binary search the minimal feasible length. To test a candidate $L$ in $O(n)$, compute a polynomial hash of every window incrementally: sliding the window drops the leftmost term and appends the rightmost. Count hashes in a map; if any hash occurs exactly once, $L$ is feasible. Using two independent moduli makes accidental collisions astronomically unlikely without any explicit verification.
s: Precompute nothing; define feasible(L): slide a window of size L across nums, maintaining two rolling hashes with different bases/mods.
Count each (hash1, hash2) pair in a hash map while sliding.
feasible(L) is true iff some pair's count equals 1.
Binary search the smallest L in [1, n] with feasible(L) = true; return it (feasible(n) always holds).
a.t: O(n log n) — each feasibility check slides a window in O(n), and binary search performs O(log n) checks.
a.sp: O(n) — the hash map holds at most n entries per check; rolling hashes are O(1).

w: In an interview, lead with the monotonicity observation (extending a unique subarray keeps it unique) — it unlocks binary search immediately. Then implement the check with rolling hashes; mention that a suffix-array/LCP approach also solves the check deterministically in O(n log n) but is far more code. Common pitfalls: forgetting that the predicate must be checked for existence (count == 1), not maximality; negative intermediate values after subtracting the outgoing term in modular arithmetic (always re-normalize with +mod); single-modulus hashing risks collisions on adversarial tests, so use two mods or verify candidates explicitly. Edge cases: n = 1 returns 1; all-equal arrays return n; arrays with any singleton value return 1. Follow-ups: solve without hashing (suffix automaton / suffix array), or report the actual subarray rather than its length (track which window achieved count 1 during the final successful check).
